task: look up specific health information online and judge its reliability (Mayo Clinic, WebMD, NIH/MedlinePlus, NHS): search a symptom, condition, or medication question, open results, distinguish reputable medical sources from ads and content farms, read the relevant section, and cross-check at least one second source; complete when the answer is on screen from an identified reputable source. Surface pinned: health-information websites reached through search. Variants: personal medical-record portals (that is a different task), telehealth appointment booking, health influencer/talking-head advice videos, and supplement marketing do not belong.

tree.label: Look up reliable health information
tree.note: do 1 - 1.4 and 1.5 only where a tool is gated (XwDq); the reference sites have no gate, and the same checker on the current site has none (1ch0). then 2, which picks 3 or 4 on a reference site or 5 on a checker; repeat 2 until a page answers - pQKZ drops the index for the search twice, FjnL drops a search for the index, y127 drops the index for the search. then 6, with 7 on the same page where the keeper does it. 8 for a second reading - FjnL runs 3 and 4 again on a second site, hIZP runs 1, 2 and 3 or 4 again on three more sites, kK4R runs 3 again, 1ch0 runs 5.2 again on the same pair, XwDq re-reads in 8.3. 8.5 loops back to 2 for the next topic - pQKZ four times - or to 5.2.5 for the next drug pair - 1ch0 three times.

children.label: Reach the health site
children.note: 1.1, 1.2 or 1.7 - every keeper arrives by address, by a library list, or by typing the site's name into Google (hIZP, three of its four sites); none types a symptom into a search engine. 1.3 whenever a banner sits on the entry page; 1.6 whenever a consent prompt, chat window or overlay covers the page - no keeper meets one. 1.4 then 1.5 only on the 2013 drugs.com (XwDq); the current drugs.com opens the same checker from a homepage tile with no registration and no terms page (1ch0). 1.5 alone where a form's Submit doubles as the terms (4Bl8).

children.label: Register an account
children.note: 1.4.1, with 1.4.2 and 1.4.3 as the form raises them, then 1.4.4; 1.4.5 when the site asks for verification after the fact. one keeper (XwDq), on the 2013 site; the reference sites never ask, and the current drugs.com runs the checker signed out (1ch0).

questions.question: The site wants an account with your age range before the tool runs. Should I create one?
questions.why: The screen shows a closed dropdown still displaying the 'Select Age' placeholder, indicating that an age range must be chosen to filter the health information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to provide their actual age, which is critical for receiving accurate and relevant medical information.
questions.check: Does the page ask for an account, with an email and an age range, before the tool will open?
questions.say_example: <Drugs.com> wants an account before it will run the checker. It asks for your email and your age range. Want me to sign up with those, or use a checker that doesn't need an account?

questions.question: Should you check the 'I am a Healthcare Professional' box?
questions.why: The screen presents an optional checkbox that, if selected, requires you to specify a job title and medical specialization.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to control the complexity of the medical content provided, as a professional profile might return highly technical clinical data instead of consumer-friendly explanations.
questions.check: Does the registration form show an optional healthcare-professional checkbox?
questions.say_example: Left the healthcare professional box unchecked.

questions.question: Which newsletters or extras should be ticked when making the account?
questions.why: The registration form includes optional checkboxes for healthcare professionals and various email newsletters that determine the type and volume of emails you will receive.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over your email inbox preferences and the accuracy of your user profile if an agent makes these selections for you.
questions.check: Which optional newsletter or marketing checkboxes does the registration form show, and are any pre-ticked?
questions.say_example: Said no to the <three> newsletters. One was ticked already, so I unticked it.

questions.question: Should I read the Terms & Conditions and Privacy Policy before agreeing to them?
questions.why: The screen requires checking a box to accept the site's terms and privacy policy, which dictate how your personal information will be handled.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to make an informed decision about whether they are comfortable with how the site collects and uses their sensitive health data.
questions.check: Does the form require accepting terms and a privacy policy to continue?
questions.say_example: Accepted the site's terms to finish signing up.

questions.question: Does the site block the tool until the email is verified?
questions.why: The screen shows a membership verification warning that restricts forum posting, prompting a decision on whether completing account setup is necessary for your current task.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to decide whether to fully activate their account for community features or bypass the interruption to quickly access the health tool.
questions.check: Does the page block the tool until the email address is verified, or does it only restrict forum posting?
questions.say_example: It won't run the checker until you click a link in the email it just sent you. Want to do that now, or should I use a checker that doesn't need an account?

questions.question: Do you agree to the checker's own terms so it will open?
questions.why: The site presents a mandatory scrollable terms text box and an 'I Agree' button specifically for the Interactions Checker, separate from the account registration terms.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to read and consent to the tool's specific medical limitations and liability waivers before relying on its health information.
questions.check: Does the tool show its own terms box with an agree button before it opens?
questions.say_example: Accepted the checker's terms. They say it's information, not medical advice.

questions.question: Does the checker open after the terms are agreed to?
questions.why: The site displays a mandatory terms of service prompt that must be accepted before granting access to the interaction checker.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to review the specific terms and conditions you are accepting before entering your health information.
questions.check: After the agree button, does the page show the checker's drug entry field, or is the terms prompt still showing?
questions.say_example: The checker didn't open after I agreed. The terms box is still up. Trying once more.

questions.question: On the cookie pop-up, do you want non-essential cookies rejected so your health query is not tracked?
questions.why: Health websites often use third-party trackers, and accepting all cookies can result in the user's sensitive medical condition being shared with data brokers and advertisers.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over their medical privacy, risking targeted advertising based on a sensitive health condition because the agent blindly clicked 'Accept All'.
questions.check: Does the cookie banner offer a reject or manage option separate from accept all?
questions.say_example: Said no to tracking cookies, so this search stays off their ad profile.

questions.question: Is a chat bubble, pop-up, or banner covering the article?
questions.why: Health websites frequently use aggressive overlays that cover the main content, requiring the user to find and click a small 'X' to read the article.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user cannot see if the agent is reading text that is actually hidden behind an overlay, or if the agent accidentally clicked a deceptive ad while trying to close the pop-up.
questions.check: Is there an overlay, chat bubble, or banner covering the article body?
questions.say_example: Closed a newsletter pop-up that was covering the article.

children.label: Search for the site by name

questions.question: Is the result being opened the real site, rather than an ad or a lookalike?
questions.why: The search results display multiple links, making it important to verify that the URL is exactly 'https://www.webmd.com' to avoid clicking on deceptive ads or unreliable content farms.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally verify the search result URL to guarantee the information will come from an authentic, reputable medical source.
questions.check: Is the result's address the site's own domain, with no Ad label on it?
questions.say_example: The first <WebMD> result is a lookalike at <webmd-health.co>. Skipping it for the real one.

children.label: Choose the way in
children.note: 2.1 on any homepage, repeatedly when the keeper tours - y127 opens four sections before choosing one. then 2.2 picks 3, 4 or 5. 2.3 whenever a route lands wrong, and it sends the task back to 2.2 - pQKZ twice, FjnL once. 2.4 when the keeper opens a homepage feature instead of a way in - pQKZ six times, each closed with the back button, none leading to 3, 4 or 5. hIZP runs 2 once per site, four times, and gives a reason each time it picks the index or a section over the search bar.

questions.question: Should I open the Interactions Checker to look up the medicine?
questions.why: The screen shows the 'Your Account' overview page with the pointer hovering over the 'Interactions Checker' link, indicating a choice of which tool to use for the query.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to choose the specific tool or section of the health website they prefer to use for their research.
questions.check: Does the site navigation show an interactions checker link?
questions.say_example: Opened the interactions checker.

questions.question: Do you want the guided symptom checker, or a plain search for the condition?
questions.why: The WebMD homepage displays a dedicated 'WebMD symptomchecker' section with an orange 'Start Now' button to begin evaluating your health issue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether to use a guided symptom checker tool or simply search for your condition manually using a search bar.
questions.check: Does the site offer both a symptom checker and a topic search?
questions.say_example: You asked what could be behind <the headache>. <WebMD> has a symptom checker for that, so I'm using it. Say search if you'd rather just read the <headache> page.

questions.question: Is this a condition question or a medicine question, so the right A to Z index gets used?
questions.why: The homepage explicitly separates 'Health A to Z' for conditions and symptoms from 'Medicines A to Z' for drug information, requiring you to choose the correct path for your query.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to specify whether you want to research a condition broadly or look up a specific medication.
questions.check: Does the site split its index into a conditions list and a medicines list?
questions.say_example: Used the medicines index, since <ibuprofen> is a drug.

questions.question: Does the body-system section that was opened actually list the condition?
questions.why: The narrator points out that using the body systems menu 'assumes that I know diabetes is a dysfunction of the endocrine system,' highlighting a prerequisite knowledge check for this navigation path.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the realization that a specific navigation path requires medical knowledge they might not have, which could lead an agent to guess or get stuck.
questions.check: Does the body-system page that was opened list the condition asked about?
questions.say_example: <Diabetes> isn't under the section I opened. I'm switching to the search box instead.

questions.question: Does the index have a general entry for the term, or only narrow ones?
questions.why: The alphabetical list displayed many specific magnesium compounds, indicating that a direct search might be better for finding a general overview.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to recognize when a site's directory is too granular and pivot to a more efficient search method.
questions.check: Does the index page show a general overview entry for the term, or only narrow entries?
questions.say_example: The index only lists specific <magnesium compounds>, so I searched instead.

questions.question: Does the site have a dedicated page for the topic, or only a passing mention?
questions.why: The text only mentions leprosy in passing while focusing broadly on general mycobacterial infections, indicating it might lack the specific depth you need.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the human judgment to quickly abandon a tangentially related article and pivot to a more focused search.
questions.check: Does the site have a page whose title is the topic asked about, or is the topic only mentioned inside a broader page?
questions.say_example: <MedlinePlus> has no page on <leprosy> itself. It only comes up inside a page on <mycobacterial infections>. I'll check <NHS> for a proper one.

children.label: Search the topic
children.note: 3.1, then 3.2 when the box offers suggestions, then 3.3 and 3.4 on the results page. 3.4 goes back to 3.1 with a different term when the pick misses - pQKZ types the common name after the technical one failed in 4. hIZP runs 3 on three of its four sites with a partial name and takes the suggestion each time.

questions.question: Did the search actually run, or is the term still sitting in the box?
questions.why: The screen shows the MedlinePlus home page with the query typed in the search bar, indicating the search has not yet been executed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to review actual health information if the agent hallucinates being on a results page before actually submitting the search.
questions.check: Does the page show a results heading or result count for the term, rather than the home page with the term still in the search box?
questions.say_example: The search never ran. The word is still sitting in the box. Pressing search now.

questions.question: What specific medical topic do you want to search for?
questions.why: Entering a precise topic into the MedlinePlus search box ensures the site retrieves the correct health information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to choose the exact symptom or condition you want to investigate.
questions.check: What term is in the search box, and on which site?
questions.say_example: Got it. Looking up <warfarin and aspirin together> on <drugs.com>, then checking it against <MedlinePlus>.

questions.question: Which suggested search term should you choose?
questions.why: The search dropdown shows both broad terms and specific subtopics like "diabetes medicines," which determines the scope of the medical information you will find.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether a broad overview or a specific subtopic best matches your actual health question.
questions.check: Does the suggestion dropdown list more than one entry containing the term, such as the plain term and subtopics?
questions.say_example: The site splits this into <diabetes>, <diabetes medicines>, and <diabetes in children>. You asked about <medicines>, so I'm taking that one. Say another if you meant something else.

questions.question: Did the search swap the term for a similar-sounding condition?
questions.why: Search engines often aggressively autocorrect complex drug names or medical conditions (e.g., changing 'hypothyroidism' to 'hyperthyroidism'), which completely changes the medical information returned.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to notice that the search results are for the wrong disease or medication entirely before clicking into them.
questions.check: Does the results heading or a 'showing results for' line contain exactly the term typed, not a different one?
questions.say_example: It changed <hypothyroidism> to <hyperthyroidism>. Those are opposite conditions. Searching the one you asked for again.

questions.question: Which kind of result should be opened, such as Health Topics or the encyclopedia?
questions.why: The search results page displayed thousands of links and specific refinement categories like 'Health Topics' and 'Medical Encyclopedia', making it important to choose the most direct path to a reliable overview.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to start with a broad summary overview or filter for specific formats like medical tests or external health links.
questions.check: Which result categories does the results page offer, such as Health Topics or Medical Encyclopedia?
questions.say_example: Took the <Health Topics> result. It's the overview page.

questions.question: Does the link chosen from the results lead to the full article on the reputable site, not an ad or a bare snippet?
questions.why: The search results display a brief summary of the condition, so you must identify the correct link to open the full article.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the chosen link leads to a comprehensive and reputable medical source instead of an ad or incomplete summary.
questions.check: Does the opened page show a full article with headings, rather than a snippet or an ad?
questions.say_example: Opened the full <MedlinePlus> article.

children.label: Browse the index
children.note: 4.1 then 4.3, or 4.2 in place of 4.1 where the site groups by body system. 4.3 lands on a page; when it is the wrong one, 2.3 takes over. pQKZ runs 4 three times and it works once; hIZP runs it once on MedlinePlus and the see-also row lands on the right page.

questions.question: When the index lists several entries for the term, which one matches what you asked?
questions.why: The screen displays a long list of health topics starting with 'D', requiring you to scroll past unrelated conditions like 'Dementia' and 'Depression' to find the exact match.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to see if the site breaks the condition down into more specific sub-categories, like Type 1 or Type 2, before clicking.
questions.check: Does the index show more than one entry containing the term, such as variants for different body parts or sub-topics?
questions.say_example: The list has <angioplasty> for the <heart>, the <legs>, and the <kidneys>. You asked about the <heart>, so that's the one. Say another if you meant a different one.

questions.question: Does the index entry send the term to a different name?
questions.why: The A-Z index lists terms like 'Halitosis' with a cross-reference to 'see Bad Breath', requiring you to click the redirected common name to find the information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to track how the medical site categorizes your specific symptom, which helps build your health literacy regarding clinical versus common terminology.
questions.check: Does the index entry for the term show a 'see' reference to another name?
questions.say_example: The site files <halitosis> under <bad breath>. Going there.

children.label: Query the interactive tool
children.note: 5.1 on a symptom checker, 5.2 on an interaction checker - the site decides which. 4Bl8 and XwDq run one check each; 1ch0 runs 5.2 four times, editing the list between runs. both end by handing a page to 6.

children.label: Describe the symptoms
children.note: 5.1.1, then 5.1.2 and 5.1.3, then 5.1.4 once per screen - nine screens for one symptom. 5.1.5 after the first list, which re-ranks it; then 5.1.6.

questions.question: What age and sex should go into the checker for the patient?
questions.why: The WebMD symptom checker requires the patient's age and gender to provide relevant results, while fields like zip code and email are optional.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might input incorrect patient demographics leading to irrelevant health information, or unnecessarily share your email address for marketing newsletters.
questions.check: Which profile fields does the symptom checker require before symptoms can be entered, and which are optional?
questions.say_example: The checker needs age and sex first. I'm putting in <6 years old>, <boy>, from what you told me. It also asks for a zip code and email. Those are optional, so I'm leaving them blank.

questions.question: Does the header above the checker show the age and sex that were entered?
questions.why: The screen displays a persistent header (e.g., 'Gender: Male', 'Age: 3-6 years') above the symptom body map, confirming the demographic filters currently applied to the tool.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to catch a silent error where the agent defaulted to an adult profile while researching a child's symptoms, which would lead to completely wrong medical triage.
questions.check: Does the header above the symptom tool show the age range and sex that were entered?
questions.say_example: The checker is set to <adult female>, but this is for your <6-year-old son>. Fixing that before anything else, since the answers change with it.

questions.question: Which entry in the symptom list matches what you described?
questions.why: The screen shows a long alphabetical list of symptoms, making it essential to select the exact match to ensure the resulting medical information is relevant.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally translate your nuanced physical feelings into the most accurate clinical term provided by the tool.
questions.check: Does the symptom list show more than one entry containing the word given?
questions.say_example: The list has <headache>, <headache, severe>, and <head pain>. I'm choosing <headache>. Say another one if that's closer to it.

questions.question: Did the symptom just picked show up in the 'Your Choices' list?
questions.why: The interface features a specific panel that tracks selected symptoms. If a click on the interactive body map or a checkbox fails to register, the symptom won't be added to this running list.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify that all their intended symptoms were actually captured by the tool before it calculates the possible conditions.
questions.check: Does the selected-symptoms panel list the symptom that was just clicked?
questions.say_example: <Headache> didn't register. The list still says none chosen. Trying again.

questions.question: The checker asks follow-up questions about the symptom. What are the answers, or should they be skipped?
questions.why: The screen offers a 'Skip Questions' button, but selecting specific options like 'about the same time of day' helps the tool narrow down the exact condition.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to provide nuanced personal details about the symptom's timing to get a highly tailored health assessment.
questions.check: Which follow-up questions does the checker show for the symptom, and is there a skip option?
questions.say_example: The checker has a few questions about <the headache>. Did it start suddenly or slowly? Is it throbbing or sharp? Mild, moderate, or severe? Answer what you know, or say skip.

questions.question: Should you add more symptoms to narrow the possible conditions?
questions.why: The screen shows 49 possible conditions for a single headache symptom, which is too broad to pinpoint the actual health issue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to provide additional, specific symptoms about the patient that an agent wouldn't know but are necessary to filter the list accurately.
questions.check: How many possible conditions does the results panel show for the symptoms entered?
questions.say_example: <Headache> alone gives <49> possible conditions. That's too many to mean much. Any other symptoms, like fever or vomiting? Or say that's all.

questions.question: Is the condition list being read the new one from after the extra symptoms went in, not the long one from before?
questions.why: The screen displays a narrowed list of three possible conditions alongside blue bars that visually indicate the probability of each ailment based on the symptoms entered.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to see how each additional symptom dynamically shifts the estimated probability of different underlying health conditions.
questions.check: Does the possible-conditions count on the page match the count after the last symptom was added?
questions.say_example: The list I was about to read is the old one. It's down to <three> now that <fever> is in. Reading the new one.

children.label: Check the drug list
children.note: 5.2.1 when the tool remembers an old list, then 5.2.2 once per drug - retyped when the box says No suggestions (1ch0). 5.2.3 only where the keeper is signed in (XwDq); 1ch0 runs every check on an Unsaved interactions list. then 5.2.4. for a follow-up question, 5.2.5 swaps one drug and returns to 5.2.4 - 1ch0 three times.

questions.question: Does the drug list still hold anything left over from an earlier check?
questions.why: The screen shows an unsaved drug list populated with previously entered medications that must be cleared using the 'New list' button to prevent them from interfering with the current search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that the agent will correctly clear out old, irrelevant data before beginning a new health inquiry.
questions.check: Does the drug list on the page contain any drug that was not asked about?
questions.say_example: The list still had <metformin> from an earlier check. I've taken it out, so the report is only about <warfarin> and <aspirin>.

questions.question: After the drug is picked from the dropdown, does it actually show up in the list, or does the list still say it is empty?
questions.why: The screen shows an empty drug name field and states your interactions list is empty, indicating that a medication must be successfully selected to proceed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the exact medication and formulation you are taking is correctly entered into the safety checker.
questions.check: After the pick, does the list show the drug name, or does it still say the list is empty?
questions.say_example: <Warfarin> didn't go in. The list still says empty. Picking it again.

questions.question: When the dropdown offers several versions of the drug, which one matches what you take?
questions.why: The search field suggests several different brands, dosages, and combination medications like Aspir 81 and Aspir-Mox, requiring a specific selection.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify the exact formulation or brand of the medication that matches your personal health inquiry.
questions.check: Does the dropdown show more than one entry for the drug name, such as brands, strengths, or combination products?
questions.say_example: The dropdown has plain <aspirin>, <Aspir 81>, and <Aspir-Mox>. The last one has an antacid mixed in. Which do you take? Say plain if it's just <aspirin>.

questions.question: When the name gets no suggestions, is the spelling off rather than the drug missing?
questions.why: Typing 'warfr' resulted in no matches, requiring the user to recognize the typo, backspace, and correct it to 'warf' to successfully locate 'warfarin'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the agent will recognize and correct a simple typo rather than falsely concluding the medication isn't in the database.
questions.check: Does the dropdown show no matches for the letters typed?
questions.say_example: No match for <warfr>. I'll try <warfarin>.

questions.question: Should the drug list be saved to the account?
questions.why: The modal offers the choice to customize the list name and save it either as a basic list or a more detailed Mednotes profile.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to organize their saved drug interactions using a custom name or an integrated health profile.
questions.check: Does the page offer to save the drug list to the account?
questions.say_example: Didn't save the drug list to the <drugs.com> account.

questions.question: Does the list show exactly the drugs asked about, before the check runs?
questions.why: The screen showed a specific list of four medications, including Amoxil and Cymbalta, queued up for an interaction check.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to verify that their exact medication list is complete and accurate before generating the interaction report.
questions.check: Which drug names does the list show before the check button?
questions.say_example: Checking <warfarin> and <aspirin>. Running it.

children.label: Edit the list for the next pair
Read the answer page
children.note: 6.1 first on every page that has one; 6.2 where the page is long; 6.3 on the encyclopedia. then 6.4, and 6.5 where the page carries them - y127 scrolls past both red boxes, hIZP reads three of them aloud. 6.6 moves to a neighbouring page and back into 6; 6.7 is reached on two pages and taken on neither. on the interaction report 6.1 is the severity tally and 6.4 is the paragraph under the badge - 1ch0 reads MANAGEMENT on the second report after skipping it on the first.

questions.question: What does the report say about this pair?
questions.why: The screen displays a section with red exclamation marks labeled 'MAJOR' for specific drug pairs, highlighting critical safety warnings that require immediate attention.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally evaluate the specific risks and warnings associated with combining your exact medications.
questions.check: What severity label does the report give for the pair, and what does its management or advice paragraph say?
questions.say_example: <Drugs.com> says <major> for <warfarin> with <aspirin>. <Together they raise the risk of bleeding.> The advice is <avoid the pair, or get blood tests more often if both are needed>.

questions.question: Which section of the page answers what was asked?
questions.why: The screen displays multiple detailed sections like 'Symptoms', 'Treatment', and 'When to See Your Doctor', requiring you to locate the exact information you need.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally absorb the nuances of the symptoms and self-care advice that might be uniquely relevant to your situation.
questions.check: Which section headings does the page show?
questions.say_example: Read the <Treatment> section, since that's what you asked about.

questions.question: Does the text under the dosage table add a limit the table doesn't show?
questions.why: The screen shows a complete table of recommended magnesium amounts by life stage, making it necessary to decide if this data alone answers the query.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses important context or warnings about the supplement if the agent exits the page without checking the detailed text.
questions.check: Does the text below the dosage table add an upper limit or condition that the table doesn't show?
questions.say_example: The table says <400 mg> a day for <adults>. The text under it adds a limit. No more than <350 mg from supplements>. That part isn't in the table.

questions.question: Does the page show an illustration the text doesn't describe?
questions.why: The screen displays both introductory text and a visual illustration of a wire mesh stent, which are crucial for fully understanding the medical procedure.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally examine the visual aid of the stent and ensure the medical explanation makes sense to you.
questions.check: Does the section include an illustration or diagram?
questions.say_example: There's a drawing here. It shows <a wire mesh tube inside the artery, holding it open>. The text doesn't say that, so that's from the picture.

questions.question: Does the reported answer keep the report's caveats and monitoring advice, not just the severity label?
questions.why: The screen details that while paracetamol is the drug of choice, the moderate interaction still requires caution and closer monitoring of INR.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally weigh the nuanced clinical caveats and monitoring recommendations provided in the interaction report.
questions.check: Does the reported answer contain the report's caveat or monitoring sentence, such as a line about caution or closer monitoring?
questions.say_example: One thing I nearly left out. It says <paracetamol> is the safer choice, but still wants your <INR> checked more often. That's part of the answer.

questions.question: When the checker finds nothing, does the page add its own warning, and a food and alcohol section?
questions.why: The screen explicitly warned that the absence of found interactions doesn't guarantee safety, and there was an ignored section for drug and food interactions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses critical safety warnings and full context, potentially leading to unsafe medical conclusions based on incomplete information.
questions.check: Does the report say no interactions were found for the drugs entered?
questions.say_example: No interactions found between <these two>. The site adds that none found doesn't mean none exist. There's also a food and alcohol section. It says <avoid grapefruit with this one>.

questions.question: Is the passage being quoted part of the article, or an ad sitting between the paragraphs?
questions.why: Health sites frequently interleave sponsored content or supplement ads directly within the article body, relying on subtle visual cues like a faint gray background or tiny 'Sponsored' text to distinguish them from the medical facts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user risks acting on biased marketing copy, mistaking a paid advertisement for objective medical advice because the agent failed to process the subtle visual boundaries.
questions.check: Is the quoted passage inside a block labeled Sponsored, Advertisement, or From our partners?
questions.say_example: The line I was about to read is an ad for a supplement, sitting between the paragraphs. Skipping it. The article itself goes on with <the next paragraph>.

questions.question: Which row of the dosage table matches the age or weight, and what dose is on it?
questions.why: Dosage instructions are often formatted in complex, multi-column tables where the relationship between a patient's weight and the correct dose is conveyed entirely through visual grid alignment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user risks administering a dangerous over- or under-dose if the agent extracts the table as flat text and misaligns the rows and columns.
questions.check: Which table row contains the weight or age given, and what dose is in that row?
questions.say_example: For a <30-pound> child the table says <5 mL> every <4 to 6 hours>. I read that off the row for <24 to 35 pounds>.

questions.question: What does the page say needs urgent medical help right away?
questions.why: The screen explicitly lists severe symptoms like bloody stools and fever that require immediate medical intervention rather than just being common, mild reactions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the personal awareness of exactly which severe symptoms to watch out for in your own body.
questions.check: Does the page show a box or list saying when to get urgent help, such as call your doctor at once, call 111, or call 999?
questions.say_example: Before the rest, the page has a get-help-now box. It says call <999> if <the rash doesn't fade under a glass> or <breathing is hard>. After that I'll read the ordinary side effects.

questions.question: Did the symptom checker trigger a 'seek emergency care immediately' red flag that halts the questionnaire?
questions.why: Entering severe symptoms like chest pain or sudden weakness often causes triage tools to lock the interface and instruct the user to call 911 rather than providing informational conditions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the critical triage context that their symptoms represent a medical emergency requiring immediate real-world action, not just further online reading.
questions.check: Does the checker show a stop or emergency message, such as seek emergency care now or call 911, in place of the conditions list?
questions.say_example: The checker stopped. With <chest pain>, it says call <911> now instead of going on. I'm stopping here too. Do you need help calling?

children.label: Judge the source
children.note: 7.5 before 1 where the narrator names the sites in advance - hIZP and 1ch0. 7.1 to 7.3 on the page in hand, in any order and rarely more than one - pQKZ reads the date, kK4R reads the providers, y127 speaks the disclaimer; hIZP and 1ch0 read neither a date nor an author on five sites. 7.4 belongs before 3.4 on any search-engine entry with a symptom as the query and never happens in this corpus.

questions.question: How recently was this medical information reviewed or updated?
questions.why: Checking the review date in the article footer ensures the health advice is current and reflects the latest medical guidelines.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the personal reassurance of seeing exactly when the medical information was last vetted by professionals.
questions.check: What review or update date does the page show, and is there a notice that the page is archived or no longer updated?
questions.say_example: This page was last reviewed in <2017>, and it says it's no longer being updated. I'll find a newer one.

questions.question: Who does the page credit for writing, reviewing, and funding it?
questions.why: The page footer explicitly lists the organizations involved in development, production, and funding, such as the Santa Clara County Library and National Network of Libraries of Medicine.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally evaluate the financial and institutional backing of the health information to judge its independence and reliability.
questions.check: Which organizations does the footer credit for writing, reviewing, or funding the page?
questions.say_example: Written by <MedlinePlus>, reviewed by <a doctor> in <2024>.

questions.question: Who provides the links in the Start Here section?
questions.why: The screen showed a 'Start Here' section with links to introductory materials from reputable organizations like the American Academy of Family Physicians.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide which specific introductory resources or providing organizations they trust most to begin their research.
questions.check: Which organizations provide the links in the Start Here section?
questions.say_example: The starting links are from <the American Academy of Family Physicians> and <NIH>.

questions.question: Does the site carry ads?
questions.why: The narrator highlights that MedlinePlus is recommended specifically 'because the site has no advertising and its information is reviewed by experts,' making ad-presence a key heuristic for reliability.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to use the presence of advertising as a personal heuristic for judging the commercial bias and reliability of a medical source.
questions.check: Does the page carry advertisement labels or an ad-free statement?
questions.say_example: <WebMD> carries ads. <MedlinePlus> has none. Used both, trusted the second more.

questions.question: Is the top of the search results an ad or an AI summary rather than a medical site?
questions.why: Searches for specific drugs often trigger ads from law firms seeking plaintiffs for side-effect lawsuits, or ads for alternative medicine, which can look like legitimate health information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to spot the 'Sponsored' tag and avoid biased or alarmist content designed to sell a service rather than inform.
questions.check: Is the top of the results page an item labeled Sponsored or Ad, or an AI-generated overview, rather than a link to a medical site?
questions.say_example: The first result is an ad from a law firm about <this drug>. Skipping it. I'm also skipping the AI summary above the links. Going to <MedlinePlus>.

questions.question: Which website should you open to check for drug interactions?
questions.why: Choosing the right website matters because you need a dedicated, reliable tool like Drugs.com to accurately check interactions between Warfarin and Aspirin as instructed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to select your preferred or most trusted medical database for evaluating specific medication interactions.
questions.check: Does the site have an interactions checker tool?
questions.say_example: Used <drugs.com> for the interaction check.

questions.question: Is the page open on one of the reputable medical sites, not a general or crowd-written one?
questions.why: The task explicitly requires using authoritative medical sources like the Mayo Clinic or NIH, whereas the screen shows a search for the crowdsourced site Wikipedia.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the guarantee of medical accuracy if the agent cross-checks health information using a user-edited encyclopedia instead of a verified medical institution.
questions.check: What site name or domain does the page header show?
questions.say_example: This is <Wikipedia>. You asked for medical sources, so I'm going to <MedlinePlus> instead.

children.label: Cross-check the answer
children.note: 8.1 or 8.2 or 8.3 as a second reading - two keepers each, and three keepers take none. hIZP is all 8.1: the same question on four sites, never compared. 1ch0 takes 8.3 as its first reading on every report and 8.2 once, to confirm a badge. 8.4 is offered on two sites and taken on neither; the one kept answer is typed onto a slide (1ch0). 8.5 closes every page and returns to 2 - pQKZ seven times - or to 5.2.5 for the next drug pair.

questions.question: Does the answer rest on one page, or has a second reputable site been read too?
questions.why: The screen shows the user opening a new tab to navigate to MedlinePlus after reviewing the first source.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the health information has been properly cross-checked against a second reputable source.
questions.check: What site does the page header show, and is it a different site from the one the answer was first read on?
questions.say_example: Checked on <drugs.com> and <MedlinePlus>. They agree.

questions.question: Does the drug information you found on this second site match what you read on the first?
questions.why: Comparing the facts between the two sources confirms whether the medical information is consistent and safe to trust.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally evaluate any subtle differences or contradictions in the medical advice provided by different sources.
questions.check: Does the second site's severity label or dosage figure match the first site's for the same pair or topic?
questions.say_example: The two sites don't agree. <Drugs.com> calls it <moderate>. <MedlinePlus> says <serious>. I'm giving you the stricter one. This is worth asking your pharmacist.

questions.question: Is the article on the second site actually just a syndicated copy of the exact same article from the first site?
questions.why: Health websites often license content from the same central databases (like Cerner Multum or HealthDay), meaning two different URLs might host the exact same text.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the realization that they haven't actually cross-checked the information against an independent medical authority, just read the same source twice.
questions.check: Does the second page carry a source credit, such as Cerner Multum or HealthDay, that matches the first page's credit?
questions.say_example: Both pages come from the same supplier, <Multum>. So that's really one source. I'll check <NHS> instead.

questions.question: On the second site, is the page for the same drug as the first, not one with a similar name?
questions.why: The screen shows 'Paracetamol' being selected from the Wikipedia search dropdown, which must perfectly align with the first source's topic to ensure a valid cross-check.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the peace of mind that the agent is consistently tracking and verifying the exact same medication across different sources without getting derailed by similar search suggestions.
questions.check: Does the second site's page title contain the same drug name as the first site's page?
questions.say_example: The second page is for <paroxetine>, not <paracetamol>. Wrong drug. Finding the right page before I compare anything.

questions.question: Do you want the consumer version or the professional one?
questions.why: The screen provides explicit options to switch between consumer and professional interaction data, which determines the complexity and depth of the medical information displayed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose the level of medical detail that best matches your personal health literacy and specific informational needs.
questions.check: Does the page offer a consumer view and a professional view?
questions.say_example: Read the consumer version of the interaction page.

questions.question: Should the report be saved or sent anywhere?
questions.why: The results page displays Email, Print, and Save options that let you keep an accurate record of the drug list to discuss with a medical professional.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose the most convenient format, such as a physical printout, for sharing these specific health findings with your doctor.
questions.check: Does the results page offer Email, Print, or Save?
questions.say_example: Didn't print or email the report. Both buttons are on the page.

questions.question: Is the quoted interaction for exactly the pair asked about, not another pair on the report?
questions.why: The slide asks if Allopurinol is a good choice for a patient taking Captopril, making it crucial to confirm that the website's 'Major' interaction warning directly addresses this exact combination.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the certainty that the final medical conclusion accurately reflects the specific patient scenario you originally needed to evaluate.
questions.check: Is the interaction entry being quoted between exactly the two drugs asked about, not a different pair on the same report?
questions.say_example: The <major> I read was for <aspirin> with <warfarin>. The pair you asked about, <allopurinol> and <captopril>, is further down and says <moderate>.
